result: STORM imaging resolved two distinct layers of agrinC within the mouse GBM, with a mean peak-to-peak distance of 132.7-137.9 nm. These agrinC layers were localized between two layers of podocalyxin (marking endothelial cells and podocytes), with agrin confirmed to be within the GBM by STORM-EM correlation.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide converging evidence from STORM imaging (C1-C3), dual-channel STORM (C4), and STORM-EM correlation (C5-C6). The quantitative measurements are consistent across 80 and 600+ regions, and the spatial relationships are validated by multiple imaging modalities including immunogold-EM.

result: AgrinN was positioned internally to agrinC layers (at -57.5 and 50.2 nm), indicating that agrin molecules are oriented perpendicular or oblique to the GBM plane with C-termini near cells and N-termini toward the GBM center. This orientation is consistent with known biochemical interactions and the ~95 nm extended conformation of agrin.
evaluation: Claims C7-C11 provide strong support through quantitative STORM measurements (C7), logical inference from spatial data (C8), and consistency with established biochemical knowledge (C9-C11). The orientation model is well-supported by both the current data and prior structural studies.

result: Integrin β1 showed two layers at -79.6 and 77.1 nm, closely overlapping with agrinC but with a slight outward shift toward cell membranes.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are supported by quantitative STORM measurements and histogram comparisons. The spatial relationship between integrin β1 and agrinC is consistent with known receptor-ligand interactions.

result: Laminin-521 (LM-521) is organized in two networks within the GBM, one from podocytes and one from endothelial cells, with C-terminal LG domains near the outer aspects (±84-88 nm) and N-terminal domains toward the center (-1.8 to -3.2 nm). The two networks overlap or are very close at the center, and laminin trimers show limited mobility across the GBM thickness.
evaluation: Claims C14-C23 provide comprehensive evidence from STORM measurements of multiple laminin domains (C14-C15, C18), transgenic mouse experiments (C18-C22), and consistency with prior structural data (C16-C17, C23). The model of two separate but overlapping networks is well-supported by cell-specific expression data.

result: Collagen α3α4α5(IV) NC1 and peri-N epitopes were broadly distributed but concentrated near the GBM center (11.92-12.5 nm). This collagen IV network is secreted solely by podocytes and forms the main network in adult GBM.
evaluation: Claims C24-C28 are supported by STORM measurements (C28) and established knowledge about collagen IV structure and expression (C24-C27). The central localization is unexpected but well-documented by the imaging data.

result: Collagen α1α1α2(IV) localized to the endothelial side of the GBM at -59.5 nm, showing a distinct distribution from collagen α3α4α5(IV). This isoform persists at low levels in adult GBM and is synthesized by endothelial cells.
evaluation: Claims C29-C34 are supported by STORM measurements (C32) and established knowledge about collagen IV isoform expression (C29-C31, C33). The distinct spatial distributions of the two collagen IV isoforms are clearly demonstrated (C34).

result: Nidogen localized to the center of the GBM at -0.22 nm, close to both collagen α3α4α5(IV) and LM-521 epitopes, consistent with its proposed role as a cross-linker.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by STORM measurements (C36) and established knowledge about nidogen structure and function (C35). The central localization is consistent with a cross-linking role, though the authors appropriately note limitations in interpretation.

result: The human GBM is at least twice as thick as mouse GBM (428 nm integrin β1 peak-to-peak distance). The increased thickness is attributed to an expanded collagen α3α4α5(IV) network and an additional central layer of LM-521. Collagen α1α1α2(IV) occupies the space between the central α3α4α5(IV) layer and the endothelial surface.
evaluation: Claims C37-C44 are supported by STORM measurements from human kidney sections (C38-C43) and comparative analysis with mouse data (C44). The structural differences between human and mouse GBM are well-documented, though the additional central LM-521 layer in human GBM requires further mechanistic explanation.

result: In the Alport syndrome mouse model (Col4a3 null), the two-layered agrinC organization was disrupted in some GBM segments, and collagen α1α1α2(IV) distribution spread across the GBM width rather than being restricted to the endothelial side. An intact collagen α3α4α5(IV) network is necessary to maintain agrin and collagen α1α1α2(IV) organization.
evaluation: Claims C45-C50 are supported by STORM imaging from knockout mice (C47-C49), established knowledge about Alport syndrome (C45-C46), and logical inference from comparative data (C50). The disruption of GBM architecture in the disease model is clearly demonstrated.

result: The GBM has a highly structured, laminated organization. Collagen α3α4α5(IV) maps to the GBM center, too distant from integrin β1 for direct interaction in human GBM. AgrinC and LMα5LG are the likely biologically relevant ligands for integrin β1, while collagen α1α1α2(IV) at the endothelial side can bind integrin β1.
evaluation: Claims C64-C68 represent key interpretations supported by the comprehensive STORM data. The spatial relationships are well-documented, and the inferences about ligand-receptor interactions are logical based on measured distances. This challenges previous assumptions about collagen IV-integrin interactions.

result: In Alport syndrome, podocytes are exposed to unfamiliar collagen α1α1α2(IV) ligands, which might lead to podocyte injury and glomerulosclerosis. Collagen α3α4α5(IV) protomers can permeate through LM-521 and agrin networks to reach the GBM center, while collagen α1α1α2(IV) forms a network near the endothelium. These different behaviors may be fundamental to GBM maintenance and related to disease pathology.
evaluation: Claims C69-C74 are largely speculative interpretations (C69-C70, C72, C74) based on the STORM data. While the spatial observations are supported (C71, C73), the mechanistic links to disease pathology and the dynamics of collagen IV movement require experimental validation beyond the current imaging data.

result: A modified Tokuyasu method with 200 nm cryosections was optimal for STORM imaging of kidney sections.
evaluation: Claim C75 is supported by empirical optimization described in the methods. This represents an important methodological advance for tissue STORM imaging.

result: Background knowledge claims about GBM composition, ECM protein structures, molecular interactions, and cell-specific expression patterns.
evaluation: Claims C51-C63 and C76 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. These provide the necessary context for interpreting the STORM data but are not novel findings of this study.
